messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 76‑year‑old electrician of South‑Asian heritage, had spent most of his life wiring buildings in the city’s downtown district. Married for more than fifty years, he and his wife, Meera, shared a modest apartment above a bakery where the scent of yeast and coffee lingered on the street. His work took him to construction sites and high‑rise elevators, a routine that had never felt risky. That routine shattered one late evening in October of 2016, when he was walking home from a job that had finished at 8 p.m. The street was dimly lit and quiet, a stark contrast to the bustle of the day. A man in a hoodie stepped out from behind a trash can and demanded Ravi’s wallet. The stranger’s voice was low, his eyes narrowed; when Ravi tried to comply, the man raised a baseball bat, brandishing it in a threatening swing. Ravi, startled, slipped and fell into a puddle of rain, feeling the sting of his cheek and the sudden shock of cold. In that moment, the world had narrowed to a single point of terror— a flash of threat that would linger for years. The next weeks were marked by an unrelenting cycle of distress. After that night, Ravi began dreaming of the encounter over and over, the bat’s metallic clang echoing each time he woke. He would find himself gasping, heart pounding, and would lay in his bed, shivering until the early hours. The dream residue, as he later called it, was a tangible reminder of that night; the memory stayed lodged in the back of his mind and would resurface whenever the darkness of night fell over his small apartment. When he awoke from a nightmare, his eyes darted to the dark corners of his room, searching for the invisible threat that had once risen from the shadows. It was in those moments of wakeful terror that he felt most unsafe, and his fear began to seep into his sense of safety during the day as well. Crowded places— the subway platform, the farmers’ market, even the small crowd of coworkers gathered for a team lunch— had long been a comfort for Ravi, a place where he felt the collective warmth of humanity. Yet after the robbery, he began to sense an undercurrent of danger within those crowds. Each hurried footstep seemed like a potential threat, each sudden motion a possible assault. The smell of alcohol in a neighboring bar, a scent that had once reminded him of family gatherings, now triggered a flash of the night’s violence; the faint odor would awaken his mind, bringing the memory of the robber’s hand and the weight of the bat to the surface. The triggers, whether a nightmare, a crowded space, or an odor, would lift the veil of normalcy, and the threat of a sudden attack would rise like a tide inside him. In a single paragraph that captured the core of his struggle, Ravi explained that the dream residue made him constantly vigilant at night. He would wake, looking for the bat, looking for the stranger’s face in the darkness. When he caught the scent of alcohol in the hallway of his apartment building, a wave of dread would crash over him, the memory of that night unfolding in his mind like a replay. In crowded areas, he’d pause, his pulse quickening as strangers moved suddenly past him, his fingers tightening on his phone in an instinctive attempt to protect himself. These triggers, each time they surfaced, pushed the sense of threat up into the foreground of his consciousness. The sense of threat— the feeling that a knife could strike at any moment, that a stranger might reach out for his wallet, that a sudden movement could hide a bat— became the loud, unrelenting note that dictated his nightly vigilance, his constant scanning for danger, and his sharp sensitivity to the slightest motion of others. For months Ravi had tried to continue his work, but the fear had begun to seep into his daily life. When he walked to the elevator on his way to the shop where he rented a small space for a toolbox, he would pause to watch the door, wary of anyone who might be near. He avoided going out after dark and would stay indoors during the evening rush, preferring the safety of his apartment’s dim hallway over the city’s bright lights. Even when his wife suggested they take a short walk to the bakery, Ravi would decline, explaining that the night still felt unsafe and that strangers could be lurking at any moment. The threat had seeped into his routine, altering his sense of security, and it was this relentless feeling that had driven him to seek help today. He had come to believe that the world had changed in that instant, that danger could lurk in the most ordinary places, and that every step carried the risk of another bat’s swing. What frightened him most was the possibility of losing that quiet routine he had built over decades, the fear of another night’s terror. He sought therapy in the hope of learning to let his mind rest, to reduce the wakeful vigilance that kept him from sleeping, and to reclaim the sense of safety he had once taken for granted. The primary reason he had finally decided to reach out was that the fear had become unmanageable; it no longer seemed like a distant echo but a constant presence that could no longer be ignored. He hoped to learn how to calm his mind after a nightmare and to feel safe in the dark again, so that the sense of threat no longer dominated his nights and his days.
